title: Shloka 142
subtitle: The ground of a false world, and a woman dancing

namas.translation: The world is false the way a snake seen in a rope is false, and she is the rope it is laid over.

morphology.note: The neuter adhiṣṭhāna takes the feminine ending in agreement with the goddess.

compound.gloss: the substratum of the unreal world

children.gloss: the moving world, all that lives

namas.translation: Release from the round of births is hers to hand out, and she hands it out freely.
Liberation is not a state she confers from outside; it is the shape she herself wears.

morphology.note: Treated as a taddhita in -in on muktirūpa, the suffix rather than the compound expressing possession; the bahuvrīhi sense, she who has liberation for her form, is the usual alternative.

namas.translation: She loves the lāsya, the graceful dance of feeling that answers Śiva's thunderous tāṇḍava.

compound.gloss: she to whom the lāsya dance is dear

children.gloss: the gentle dance expressing love, danced by women

namas.translation: When the time comes she folds the worlds back into herself, and nothing resists.
She is the reticence that keeps a thing worth having out of plain sight.

namas.gloss: Praised By Rambhā And The Apsarases
namas.translation: Rambhā and the other dancers of Indra's court bow before a beauty they cannot match.

compound.gloss: saluted by Rambhā and the rest

children.gloss: Rambhā, the loveliest of the celestial nymphs
beginning; and so on, and the rest

commentary.meaning: The verse is built out of two alliterative triads and they pull in opposite directions. The first line is three names beginning with m, and it is the most technically Vedāntic sentence in the hymn: the world is mithyā, only apparent, and she is its adhiṣṭhāna, the real thing underneath on which the appearance rests; she gives release; she is release. The second line is three names beginning with l, and it abandons philosophy for a court. She loves the lāsya, the graceful dance; she brings about laya; she is modesty. Then a seventh name from outside both patterns has Rambhā and the other celestial dancers bowing to her. The hinge is laya, which in this literature means the dissolution of the worlds and in music means tempo — so the name placed between a dance and a display of bashfulness quietly says that the ending of everything is the measure the dance is kept to. The verse does not resolve its two halves. It puts the emptiest possible metaphysics and the most embodied possible image side by side and lets the reader see that they are being said of the same person.
commentary.history:
Mithyā and adhiṣṭhāna are not loose words: they belong to the analysis Advaita Vedānta gives of error. When a rope in dim light is taken for a snake, three things are true at once: the snake is not simply nonexistent, since it is seen and produces fear; it is not real either, since it vanishes on inspection; and it could not have appeared without something actually there for it to appear on. Mithyā names the peculiar status of the snake, neither real nor unreal, and adhiṣṭhāna names the rope — the substratum on which a superimposition is laid. Śaṅkara opens his commentary on the Brahmasūtras with an extended treatment of exactly this, since the world is held to stand to brahman as the snake stands to the rope.

The name puts the goddess in the position of the rope, and the consequence is the opposite of nihilism: an illusion requires a reality to borrow from, and the more thoroughly the world is called false the more weight is thrown onto whatever underlies it. The name thus makes a claim about her substantiality by way of a claim about the world's insubstantiality. It is also, for a Śākta hymn, a considerable doctrinal borrowing: Śrīvidyā in its later South Indian forms was carried largely by brahmins who were also Advaitins, and names like this one are the seam where the two vocabularies were joined.

Muktidā and muktirūpiṇī work as a pair, and the second corrects the first. Mukti, from √muc, to loose or release, is liberation from the round of births; a giver of liberation is an agent producing an effect, and any effect, in the standard argument, is a made thing and therefore perishable. If liberation were handed over it could in principle be lost. Saying that she is liberation removes it from the category of things given and received.

With the second line the register changes completely. Lāsya is a dance. In later and popular usage it is the gentle, lyrical dance of women, set against the tāṇḍava, the violent dance of Śiva, the two taken as a matched pair belonging to the goddess and the god. This neat opposition is a crystallisation: in Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra the terms are more technical and less tidily gendered, and the familiar picture owes as much to later poetry and iconography as to the treatise. The picture is nonetheless the one the hymn assumes, and the Saundaryalaharī has a celebrated verse in which the two dance together at the base of the spine.

Layakarī follows, and the word laya is doing double duty. Cosmologically it is dissolution, the reabsorption of the manifest world at the end of a cycle, the sense it has in pralaya; later yoga literature also names a layayoga among its divisions. But laya is equally the ordinary term for tempo in Indian music, and a name meaning she who makes the laya, standing immediately after a name about dancing, cannot help carrying it. The pun is not frivolous. It states in one word what the image of the dancing deity exists to state: what looks like the end of the world from inside it is, from her side, the beat.

Lajjā is a bare abstract noun standing alone as a name, which is unusual in this hymn and has a specific precedent. The Devī Māhātmya's litany in its fifth chapter salutes the goddess as abiding in all beings in the form of one quality after another — consciousness, sleep, hunger, patience, error — and modesty is among them. Behind the name there is probably also a mantra. The syllable hrīṃ, which closes each of the three segments of the fifteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā mantra, is known in mantra literature as the lajjā-bīja, the seed-syllable of modesty, from hrī, shame or bashfulness. A hymn that elsewhere describes the mantra's syllables is very likely doing so here. Read either way, the name has a point beyond decorum: modesty keeps a thing covered, which is what a mystery requires, and the hymn has already said that her form is guhya, to be kept hidden.

Rambhādivanditā closes the verse and returns it to the dance. Rambhā is the foremost of the apsarases, the celestial nymphs who came out of the churned ocean and dance in Indra's court; her name stands for the class, and ādi, and the rest, does the rest of the work. The compound is passive — she is the one saluted by them — and the choice is pointed, because the apsarases are the professionals. Having called her fond of the lāsya, the hymn has the best dancers in the three worlds bow to her, a compliment paid in the currency of the previous name rather than a generic statement that everyone worships her.
commentary.practice:
The verse falls into eight, three, five in the first line and four, four, two, six in the second, and the alliteration makes it easy to hold: three names on m, then three on l, then one on r. Reciters who lose the thread usually do so in the second line, where lāsyapriyā and layakarī are metrically identical four-syllable words beginning with la-. Fix the order by sense — the dance first, then the tempo it is danced to — and the transposition stops.

Mithyājagadadhiṣṭhānā is the hardest word in the verse and is best learned as three pieces. Mithyā opens with the cluster thy, an aspirated dental followed by the palatal glide, with the aspiration genuinely released. Jagat, the moving world, is a t-stem, and before the vowel that follows its final t voices to d, which is why the name reads jagad-adhiṣṭhānā. Adhiṣṭhāna is adhi plus sthāna, standing-place, and the s of sthāna has become the retroflex ṣ under a regular rule of internal sandhi; the ṭh that follows has been drawn back to match it. So the cluster ṣṭh is two retroflexes in a row, tongue-tip curled back for both, with a puff of breath on the second.

Muktidā and muktirūpiṇī share the cluster kt, a velar stop closing directly onto a dental with no vowel between. The ṇ of rūpiṇī is retroflex; a dental n there is the usual error.

In lāsyapriyā the sy is a dental sibilant plus the palatal glide, and the pr of priyā is not the English pr but a labial stop followed by a distinct trilled or tapped r. Lajjā has a genuinely doubled j and must be held: laj-jā, with the closure sustained across the join. Rambhādivanditā begins with the labial nasal before the aspirated bh, and hides a small sandhi in the middle: rambhā plus ādi, a long ā meeting a long ā, giving the single long ā of rambhādi.

For recitation as archanā, with each name in the dative followed by namaḥ: mithyājagadadhiṣṭhānāyai, muktidāyai, muktirūpiṇyai, lāsyapriyāyai, layakaryai, lajjāyai, rambhādivanditāyai. Five ā-stems taking -āyai and two ī-stems contracting to -yai, and the two contracted forms are not adjacent, so the pattern has to be learned rather than felt.

The demand this verse makes is that its two halves be chanted in the same voice. There is a temptation to give the first line the gravity of philosophy and the second line the lightness of ornament, as though the dancing and the modesty and the applauding nymphs were a relaxation after the hard part. The verse is constructed against that reading. It places laya between the dance and the modesty precisely so that the dissolution of the worlds sits inside the description of a performance, and it places the giver of liberation next to the ground of an unreal world so that the metaphysics is not left to stand on its own either. Someone chanting this at speed passes through the whole of Advaita Vedānta and the whole of the celestial court in eight seconds. The verse is not asking for that to be resolved into a single tone. It is asking for both to be said.

crossReferences.deva: नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः । उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः ॥
crossReferences.iast: nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ | ubhayor api dṛṣṭo'ntas tv anayos tattvadarśibhiḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: Of what is not there is no coming to be; of what is there is no ceasing to be. The settled conclusion about both has been seen by those who see how things are.
crossReferences.relevance: The sentence Advaita builds its account of the world on, and the presupposition of mithyājagadadhiṣṭhānā. If the unreal cannot come into existence and the real cannot go out of it, then an apparent world that plainly does both requires a third status, which is what mithyā names, and a permanent substratum, which is what adhiṣṭhāna names. The verse also connects this shloka back to the earlier name bhāvābhāvavivarjitā, since it is working with the same pair of terms.

crossReferences.deva: तवाधारे मूले सह समयया लास्यपरया नवात्मानं मन्ये नवरसमहाताण्डवनटम् । उभाभ्यामेताभ्यामुदयविधिमुद्दिश्य दयया सनाथाभ्यां जज्ञे जनकजननीमज्जगदिदम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: tavādhāre mūle saha samayayā lāsyaparayā navātmānaṃ manye navarasamahātāṇḍavanaṭam | ubhābhyām etābhyām udayavidhim uddiśya dayayā sanāthābhyāṃ jajñe janakajananīmaj jagad idam ||
crossReferences.translation: At your base, at the root centre, I contemplate the Nine-natured one, dancer of the great tāṇḍava of the nine rasas, together with Samayā who is intent on the lāsya. From these two, joined and moved by compassion toward the act of arising, this world was born, possessed of a father and a mother.
crossReferences.relevance: The fullest statement in the tradition of what lāsyapriyā assumes: her dance and his are not two performances but one, and the world is their offspring. The verse also supplies the link this shloka makes obliquely between dancing and cosmic process, since here the dance is at the origin of the world where layakarī places it at the end. Note that the poem calls her Samayā, the technical designation of the goddess in the internalised branch of Śrīvidyā practice.

crossReferences.source: Devī Māhātmya, chapter 5 (from the litany of the goddess as universally present; verse numbering varies between editions)
crossReferences.deva: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु लज्जारूपेण संस्थिता । नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमो नमः ॥
crossReferences.iast: yā devī sarvabhūteṣu lajjārūpeṇa saṃsthitā | namas tasyai namas tasyai namas tasyai namo namaḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: The goddess who abides in all beings in the form of modesty — to her homage, to her homage, to her homage, homage upon homage.
crossReferences.relevance: The precedent for lajjā standing alone as a name. The Devī Māhātmya's litany runs through consciousness, intelligence, sleep, hunger, shadow, power, thirst, patience, error and a dozen more, treating each as a form in which she is present in every creature, and modesty is one of them. That litany is the reason a single abstract noun can function as a divine name in this hymn without further explanation: the move had already been made, in a text every reciter of the sahasranāma would have known.

references.title: Brahma-Sūtra-Bhāṣya of Śrī Śaṅkarācārya
references.author: tr. Swāmī Gambhīrānanda (Advaita Ashrama, Calcutta)
references.note: Read only the opening section on superimposition, which runs a few pages and is the source of everything this verse's first name assumes. Śaṅkara's care in distinguishing what is superimposed from what it is superimposed on is exactly the distinction that makes adhiṣṭhāna a compliment to the goddess rather than a dismissal of the world.

references.title: Advaita Vedānta: A Philosophical Reconstruction
references.author: Eliot Deutsch (University of Hawaii Press, 1969)
references.note: Short, lucid and unusually good on the status of mithyā, which most introductions either translate as illusion and leave alone or turn into an assertion that nothing exists. Deutsch takes seriously that the term is defined negatively against both existence and non-existence, which is what makes the rope-and-snake analysis work.

references.title: The Nāṭyaśāstra, ascribed to Bharata-muni
references.author: tr. Manomohan Ghosh (Asiatic Society / Chowkhamba)
references.note: Worth consulting to see how much the familiar tāṇḍava-and-lāsya opposition owes to later tradition rather than to the treatise itself. The technical use of lāsya in the text is narrower and stranger than the popular one, and knowing this keeps the name from being read as a simple picture of a woman dancing prettily.

references.title: Tantric Mantras: Studies on Mantraśāstra
references.author: André Padoux (Routledge, 2011)
references.note: For the reading of lajjā as a reference to the syllable hrīṃ. Padoux explains how seed-syllables acquire conventional names drawn from the words they are extracted from, which is the mechanism by which a word for modesty can also be the standard designation of the most important sound in this tradition.

references.title: Lalitā-sahasranāma, with Bhāskararāya's commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Adyar Library and Research Centre)
references.note: The place to see how a commentator handles a verse that changes register halfway through. The traditional method is to refuse the change — to find a mantric or philosophical sense in lajjā and rambhādivanditā as readily as in mithyājagadadhiṣṭhānā — and whether or not one accepts the individual readings, the refusal is instructive.
